Working in Teams
Industry expectations from software engineers include good technical capability, problem-solving, communication, and team working capabilities. Team effectiveness directly affects project output (productivity and quality). The 'genius programmer' is a myth; projects succeed due to their teams.

Effective Teams
Two key dimensions of an effective team: Stakeholder satisfaction (users/sponsors are happy with the outcome) and Team satisfaction (team members are motivated). Self-managing teams have the autonomy to decide how they work (culture, task allocation, quality) within external constraints.

The Three Pillars (HRT)
- Humility: You are not infallible; there is scope for improvement. Do not identify yourself strictly with your code.
- Respect: Care about others in the team, appreciate their abilities, and criticize the output, never the person.
- Trust: Believe that others will do the right things for the project, maintain fairness, and keep workloads even.

Teamworking Culture & Leadership
Synchronous (short, focused meetings) and asynchronous (issue trackers, emails, slack) communication are key. A Team Leader (TL) should drive the project, build consensus, resolve conflicts, and not act like a boss. At the end of projects/milestones, a 'lessons learned' session helps identify what worked and what needs changing.

Software Project Management
The development process is the central process. Project management involves Planning and Monitoring/Control. Planning includes Cost and schedule estimation, Quality planning, and Risk management.

Effort Estimation
Effort estimation (often in person-months) is key to planning. Estimation accuracy improves with more information about the project (illustrated by the Cone of Uncertainty). 
Models:
- Top-down Estimation: Estimates total effort first, then components. Uses overall size. Formula: $Effort = a * size^b$ (E is in person-months, size in KLOC; constants a and b determined through regression analysis). COCOMO is a top-down model that adjusts initial estimates using 15 cost driver attributes.
- Bottom-up Estimation: Effort for components/phases estimated first, then aggregated. Can use activity-based costing.

Scheduling
Schedules exist at two levels: Overall schedule (major milestones) and Detailed schedule (assignment of lowest-level tasks to resources). Overall schedule can be estimated using Effort (e.g., COCOMO: $S = 2.5 * E^{0.38}$). Detailed schedules (e.g., using MS Project) evolve and track % completion.

Quality Planning
Goal: Low delivered defect density (#defects/KLOC). Defects are injected at any stage and removed primarily via Quality Control (QC) activities like reviews and testing. Cost of fixing a defect increases exponentially with latency (time taken to find it). Early defect removal is emphasized.

Risk Management
Risk is any uncertain event that can cause project failure. Identification uses checklists and past experience (e.g., Top risks: manpower shortage, changing requirements, unrealistic schedules). Prioritization: Classify probability and impact (Low, Medium, High) and focus on High-High or High-Medium risks for mitigation.

Software Process Models
A process model specifies a generic set of stages. 
Effort Distribution: Req (10-20%), Design (10-20%), Coding (20-30%), Testing (30-50%). Coding is not the most expensive phase.
- Waterfall: Linear sequence (Req -> HLD -> DD -> Code -> Test -> Deploy). Good for simple, clear projects. Bad for changing requirements ('all or nothing').
- Prototyping: Builds a quick/dirty version to understand requirements, alleviating requirements risk.
- Iterative: Sequence of waterfalls. Feedback from one iteration used in future ones. Avoids feature bloat.
- Timeboxing: Iterations with fixed durations. Features are adjusted to fit the schedule. Can pipeline stages for parallel execution.

Open Source Software (OSS) Processes
OSS has a Conception stage (initial working prototype) and a Community stage. The team consists of core developers (highly active, write ~80% of new features), active/peripheral contributors, and users. 
- Requirements: Managed as Modification Requests (MRs) via issue/bug logs (e.g., Bugzilla).
- Work Assignment: Voluntary. Core developers usually tackle their 'owned' modules.
- Code Management: Central repository. Changes done locally, tested, and submitted as 'patches' for review by core devs.
- Release: A release manager freezes features, then code, and coordinates testing.
- Lessons Learned: 'Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow' (Linus's Law). Users are treated as co-developers. Release early and often.

Agile Development
A response to document-heavy, rigid commercial processes. 
Agile Manifesto values: Working software over comprehensive documentation, Customer collaboration over contract negotiation, Responding to change over following a plan, Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.
Extreme Programming (XP) Practices:
- PM Practices: Small cross-functional teams, open office, planning game (release and iteration planning via user stories), daily stand-up meetings, 40-hr week, on-site customer.
- Technical Practices: Pair programming, Test-Driven Development (TDD), Continuous Integration (CI), Simple/incremental design, Refactoring, Shared code (collective ownership).
prerequisite_gaps: Regression analysis (mentioned for determining constants a and b in COCOMO without explanation).
Cone of Uncertainty (diagram shown with multipliers 4x to 0.25x without explicit naming or statistical background).
CVS and Version Control Systems (assumed knowledge for OSS code management).
Refactoring (briefly mentioned in Agile as 'changing design without changing functionality' but lacking technical depth on how it's executed).

section_map.section_content:
Industry expectations from software engineers: Good technical capability and ability to learn, problem-solving, communication, and team working capabilities. Team effectiveness directly affects the project output - productivity and quality. Genius programmer is a myth; projects succeed due to their teams. A project can easily fail due to ineffective teams. What is an effective team? A. Stakeholder satisfaction (users/sponsors are satisfied with outcome). B. Team satisfaction (members are motivated). Self-Managing Teams: How a team works is decided by the team itself. Decisions about culture, task allocation, quality taken by the team. Requires autonomy.

The Three Pillars (HRT):
1. Humility: you are not infallible; scope for improvement; equal to others. Don't identify yourself with your code.
2. Respect: genuinely care about others in team; criticize output, never the person. Listen to others.
3. Trust: Believe others will do the right things. Deliver work on time. Fair decision-making.

Team Culture: Shared values and goals, process of doing work, and behavioral practices. Communication is key: Synchronous (short regular stand-up meetings) and Asynchronous (issue trackers, comments). Team Leader is a catalyst, not a boss, sets clear goals, resolves conflicts, and does not ignore non-performers.

Project management is the process to manage the development process, risks, and customer management. Two broad phases: Planning and Monitoring/Control. Planning occurs initially (Cost/schedule estimation, Quality planning, Risk plans). 

Effort Estimation: Essential for schedule and cost. Estimation accuracy improves with more project information (Early estimates are inaccurate, represented by a funnel graph from 4x to 0.25x variance across phases like Feasibility, Req Analysis, System Design, Coding). 
- Top-down Estimation: Determines total effort, then component effort. $Effort = a * size^b$ (E in person-months, size in KLOC, constants determined via regression). COCOMO uses size but adjusts using 15 multiplying cost-driver factors (e.g., Reliability, Complexity, Analyst capability).
- Bottom-up Estimation: Effort for components estimated first, then total. Uses activity-based costing.

section_map.section_title: Scheduling, Quality Planning, and Risk Management
section_map.section_content:
Project Schedule: Exists at two levels. Overall schedule (major milestones, e.g., $S = 2.5 * E^{0.38}$) and Detailed schedule (lowest level tasks assigned to resources, e.g., Unit Test taking 1 day, 7 hrs effort).

Quality Planning: Goal is low delivered defect density (#defects/KLOC). Defects are injected at any stage and removed via Quality Control (QC) - reviews and testing. Cost of defect increases with latency (fixing in operation is 100x more expensive than in requirements phase). Early defect removal is essential.

Risk Management: Risk is an uncertain event causing project failure. Identification relies on checklists (Top risks: Shortage of trained manpower, changing requirements, unrealistic schedules). Prioritization: Classify Probability (L, M, H) and Impact (L, M, H). Focus on HH or HM/MH risks. Mitigation involves planned steps (e.g., tackling manpower attrition by rotating jobs and keeping backups).

Project Tracking: Monitoring using measurements (effort, size, defects). Done via Activity-level tracking (% complete), Status reports (weekly), and Milestone analysis.

Software Process: A set of steps to produce software. Distribution of effort: Req (10-20%), Design (10-20%), Coding (20-30%), Testing (30-50%). Coding is not the most expensive. Defect distribution is highest in Coding (50+%).

Process Models:
- Waterfall: Linear sequence (Req -> HLD -> DD -> Code -> Test -> Deploy). Strict phases, document-heavy. Good for well-understood problems. Weakness: 'All or nothing' delivery, assumes requirements freeze early.
- Prototyping: Builds prototype to understand requirements. Feedback improves reqs. 'Quick and dirty' code, thrown away or heavily modified. Reduces risk for novice users.
- Iterative Development: Sequence of waterfalls. Delivers software in increments. Feedback from one iteration used in the next. Avoids feature bloat. Weakness: System architecture may suffer without full upfront planning.
- Timeboxing: Fix iteration duration, determine specs to fit. Pipeline execution of stages (e.g., Req, Build, Deploy overlapping across timeboxes). Good for strict deadlines.

Most OSS are not commissioned; started by a few programmers creating an initial working prototype (Conception Stage). It then transitions to a Community Stage. 
Team: Highly distributed globally, async communication. Roles include Project Leader, Core Developers (~15 people, write 80% features, 2/3 bug fixes), active/peripheral contributors, users. 
Requirements: Treated as Modification Requests (MRs) in an issue/bug log (e.g., Bugzilla). 
Work Assignment: Volunteers pick issues. Core devs review and approve 'patches' before committing to the central CVS repository.
Release Management: A release manager freezes features/code and stabilizes the build. 
Case Studies: Apache (Apache Group votes on major changes) and Mozilla (Netscape origin, uses Bugzilla, paid core devs). 
Motivations: Extrinsic (reputation, career) and Intrinsic (fun, ideals). Firms contribute to build service businesses. 
Lessons Learned: 'Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow' (Linus's Law). Treat users as co-developers. Debugging is highly parallelizable.

A response to document-heavy, rigid commercial processes from the 1990s. Agile views software development as an evolution, utilizing short timeboxed iterations (1-4 weeks).
Agile Manifesto Values: 
1. Working software over comprehensive documentation.
2. Customer collaboration over contract negotiation.
3. Responding to change over following a plan.
4. Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.

Extreme Programming (XP) Practices:
- Project Management (PM) Practices: Small cross-functional teams, open office, continuity, on-site customer representative. Planning Game (Release planning with user stories sorted by risk/value; Iteration planning breaking stories into tasks). Daily stand-up meetings. 40-hour work week.
- Technical Practices: User stories (high-level requirements), Test-Driven Development (TDD - write tests before code), Continuous Integration (CI - code checked in daily, builds automatically), Pair Programming (two devs, one screen), Simple incremental design, Refactoring (changing design without altering functionality), Shared Code (collective ownership).

extracted_pyqs: Exercise - Estimation: Suppose an application to be built has a front end component of est size 2000 LOC of JS code, and a backend component with est size of about 5000 LOC of Java code. Using top-down approach, estimate how much effort will building this application take. Make any assumptions you need and state them.

Exercise - Bottom Up Estimation: Suppose the appl has: 10 screens in FE and 10 APIs at the back - half simple and half complex. Using bottom-up approach, estimate how much total effort will building this application take. Make any assumptions you need and state them.

Exercise questions: Which of these is not true (tick all)? a) To control cost, quality and schedule of a project, we must use a good process b) Main focus of software engineering is to make people more efficient using good processes and technology c) It is best to find a defect as close as possible to the point of its injection d) Development process and testing/bug management are the most important processes in a project.

Question... Which of these is true (tick all that apply)? a) The most time consuming phase is coding b) If it takes more effort to write code that can be tested easily, the extra effort is worth it c) Fixing defects in requirements towards the end of development is extremely expensive d) Code should be written so it can easily understood and can be easily modified e) Good programming ability is important for doing requirements analysis.

Questions... 1. What are the main goals / driving forces of a project (a few words) 2. If the same number of defects in each phase remain in the software at delivery, defects in which phase will be most expensive to remove 3. Which is the most expensive phase / activity in a software development project 4. Over the life of a software, what is the most expensive activity.

Questions... Which process model is most suitable for (give a reason also): 1. An office wants to automate its existing manual process for handling claims. 2. A new platform is to be built to enable students to mentor other students. 3. An application where the logic / functionality is clear, but there is uncertainty about the user interface. 4. For the project you are thinking of, if you have full freedom (i.e. no SDOS constraints) - give 3 reasons for this.
Discussion: Why do individuals contribute to OSS (for free)? Why do corporates contribute to OSS?
Exercise: Work with your group – write the open source development process for one release as an algorithm.
